entry: Leader of the [[First Crusade]] and first ruler of the [[Kingdom of Jerusalem]] (1099–1100). The second son of Eustace II, Count of Boulogne, he became lord of Bouillon, in present-day [[Belgium]], in 1076 through his mother's family. In 1087 Emperor Henry IV confirmed him as Duke of Lower Lorraine, as a reward for his support during the Great Saxon Revolt. He joined the First Crusade in 1096 and played a key role in the capture of [[Jerusalem]] in 1099. When Raymond IV, Count of Toulouse, declined the offer to rule the new kingdom, Godfrey accepted, though he was reluctant to take the title of king. He ruled as prince under the title *Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri* (Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre). He secured the kingdom by defeating the Fatimids at Ascalon a month later. He was succeeded by his brother Baldwin as King of Jerusalem.

1954 Japanese [[Kaiju|kaiju]] film directed by Ishirō Honda, with special effects by Eiji Tsuburaya. Produced and distributed by [[Toho]], it is the first film in the Godzilla franchise. Japanese authorities confront a gigantic monster mutated by nuclear bomb testing. The production pioneered suitmation, in which a performer in a suit interacts with miniature sets. Premiering in [[Nagoya]] on October 27, 1954, it received mixed reviews but was a box-office success. The 1956 American version, *Godzilla, King of the Monsters!*, heavily re-edited the film and added new footage of [[Raymond Burr]]. [[Guinness World Records|Guinness World Records]] later recognized the franchise as the longest-running film franchise.

Fictional giant monster (daikaijū) first seen in the [[Godzilla (1954 film)|1954 film]] of the same name. It became an international pop culture icon, starring in 33 Japanese films by [[Toho]], five American films and numerous games, novels and comics. Originally 50 m tall, later versions are mostly 100 m, as tall as [[Skyscraper|skyscrapers]]. A prehistoric reptilian monster awakened by nuclear testing, it was conceived as a metaphor for [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]]; others read it as a metaphor for the United States. Its epithet, King of the Monsters, first appeared in the 1956 American version, *Godzilla, King of the Monsters!*

Tragic play in two parts by [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]], based on the German folk legend of [[Faust]]. Nearly all of Part One and most of Part Two are in rhymed verse. Although rarely staged in full, it has the largest audience numbers on German-language stages, and many regard it as Goethe's magnum opus and a major work of [[German literature]]. Goethe developed the earliest form, the *Urfaust*, between 1772 and 1775; its manuscript is lost, but a copy was found in 1886. *Faust, a Fragment* appeared in print in 1790, and Part One was published in 1808 and revised in 1828–29. Goethe finished Part Two in 1831; it was published posthumously the following year. Part One follows Faust's pact with Mephistopheles, the [[Devil]], and the tragic seduction of Gretchen. Part Two moves from Faust's soul to social phenomena such as psychology, history and politics.

Basaltic plateau in southwestern [[Syria]], most of which [[Israel]] has occupied and administered since the 1967 [[Six-Day War]]. Israel applied its law to the area in 1981, a move described as annexation and condemned as illegal by the [[United Nations Security Council|UN Security Council]]. The United States recognized Israeli sovereignty in 2019, and Colombia in 2026; the international community largely regards the territory as Syrian land under occupation. Israel cites security concerns, given the heights' overlook of the Sea of Galilee. After the [[Syrian civil war]] began in 2011, the Syrian-held part was split between government and opposition forces, and Israeli forces took control of the UN buffer zone in late 2024.

Coastal city and region in [[Queensland]], Australia (pop., 2024: 681,389), about 66 km south-southeast of [[Brisbane]]. It is Queensland's second-largest city and the most populous non-capital city in Australia. The area was home to the Yugambeh people, and the city grew from small townships, the earliest being Nerang in 1865. Tourism drove growth from the 1920s. The city was declared in 1959, and its first high-rise was built in 1960. The 1980s boom, marked by skyscraper construction, was also associated with organized crime, particularly the [[Yakuza|yakuza]] and the Russian mafia. Since the early 21st century the city has been a major film and television production center, nicknamed Goldywood. Its GDP was AU$55.1 billion as of 2025.

Discovery of [[Gold|gold]] that brings an onrush of miners seeking their fortune. Major 19th-century gold rushes took place in [[Australia]], Greece, Venezuela, New Zealand, [[Brazil]], [[Chile]], South Africa, the United States and [[Canada]]. Gold mining itself proved unprofitable for most miners, but some amassed fortunes, and merchants and transport companies made large profits. The increased gold supply stimulated global trade and investment, and rushes spurred immigration that often led to permanent settlement. A typical rush moved from placer mining, washing gold from gravel with pans and sluice boxes, to larger organizations and tunnels, and eventually to lode mining. Gold rushes occurred as early as ancient Greece. The [[California|California]] Gold Rush, begun in 1848 when James W. Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill, drew an estimated 300,000 migrants and speeded California's admission as a state in 1850. Later, the Klondike rush in Canada's [[Yukon|Yukon]] ran from 1896 to 1899.

Ukrainian-born Israeli stateswoman, prime minister of Israel from 1969 to 1974 and its first female head of government. Raised in [[Milwaukee]] after emigrating in 1906, she embraced Labor Zionism, settled in [[Mandatory Palestine]] in 1921 and joined a [[Kibbutz|kibbutz]]. She signed Israel's Declaration of Independence in 1948 and served as Labor Minister, then Foreign Minister, until 1966. Israel was caught off guard by the [[Yom Kippur War]] in 1973, and public anger over early losses led to an inquiry. After her Alignment coalition lost its majority, she resigned in 1974 and was succeeded by [[Yitzhak Rabin]]. Admirers credit her with helping found the state; critics blame her for the war's surprise and for dismissive statements about Palestinians. Most historians consider her more effective as minister than as premier.

Unproven claim in [[Number theory|number theory]] that every even [[Natural number|natural number]] greater than 2 is the sum of two [[Prime number|prime numbers]]. It is one of the oldest and best-known unsolved problems in [[Mathematics|mathematics]]. Christian Goldbach proposed related ideas in a 1742 letter to [[Leonhard Euler]], who replied that he regarded the two-prime form as a completely certain theorem he could not prove. The conjecture has been shown to hold for all natural numbers below 4×10¹⁸. Olivier Ramaré showed in 1995 that every even number of at least 4 is the sum of at most six primes. Harald Helfgott proved the weak form, that every odd integer greater than 5 is the sum of three primes, in 2013.

Suspension bridge across the Golden Gate [[Strait|strait]], linking [[San Francisco]] to Marin County, [[California]]. The one-mile-wide strait connects San Francisco Bay to the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]]. The bridge carries U.S. Route 101 and California State Route 1 and is part of U.S. Bicycle Route 95. Many experts had said a bridge could not be built across the strait's strong tides and winds, but it opened to the public on May 27, 1937. Chief engineer Joseph Strauss led the project, with Leon Moisseiff, Irving Morrow and Charles Ellis contributing to the design. At its opening it was the world's longest and tallest suspension bridge, records lost in 1964 and 1998. Its main span is 4,200 feet (1,280 m), and its [[Art Deco]] towers rise 746 feet (227 m).

Mongol-founded khanate in the northwestern part of the [[Mongol Empire|Mongol Empire]], later Turkicized. Originally made up of lands granted to Jochi, it grew greatly under [[Batu Khan]]. Its military power peaked under Özbeg Khan (1312–1341), who adopted Islam. At its height its territory extended from Siberia and Central Asia across Eastern Europe to the Danube, and from the [[Black Sea]] to the [[Caspian Sea]]. After the Great Troubles (1359–1381) and [[Timur]]'s 1396 invasion, it broke into smaller khanates. [[Moscow]] defeated the Horde at the Great Stand on the Ugra River in 1480, traditionally marking the end of Mongol rule over Russia. The [[Crimean Khanate]] and [[Kazakh Khanate]], its last remnants, survived until 1783 and 1847, when Russia conquered them.

British breed of retriever dog of medium-large size. It is known for a gentle, affectionate nature and a striking golden coat. It is a working dog, and registration requires successful completion of a working trial; it is also a common companion and guide dog. Sir Dudley Marjoribanks, later Baron Tweedmouth, developed the breed at his Guisachan estate in Scotland in the late 19th century, crossing Flat-coated Retrievers with Tweed Water Spaniels and, in some lines, Red Setter, [[Labrador Retriever]] and [[Bloodhound]]. The Kennel Club recognized it in 1913, and it spread to many parts of the world during the interwar period.

Principle of treating others as one would want to be treated by them, also called an ethics of reciprocity. Its positive form directs one to treat others as one would like to be treated; its negative form, sometimes called the Silver Rule, asks only that one not harm others. The negative form appears in a Late Period Egyptian papyrus, the [[Analects|Analects]] of [[Confucius]], ancient Greek philosophy, the teachings of Hillel the Elder, and Buddhist and Jain scripture. In Confucianism, the negative formulation is combined with positive duties. Versions of the rule appear in most religions and creeds, in China, the [[Indian subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]], the Near East and the Greco-Roman world. The term Golden Rule came into wide use in early 17th-century Britain, where Anglican theologians used it.

Gurdwara in [[Amritsar]], [[Punjab, India|Punjab]], India, the pre-eminent spiritual site of [[Sikhism]]. The complex surrounds the sanctum and the Amrit Sarovar, a sacred pool. Guru Ram Das completed the pool in 1577, and Guru Arjan placed a copy of the Adi Granth in the temple in 1604. [[Sikh Empire|Maharaja Ranjit Singh]], founder of the Sikh Empire, rebuilt it in marble and copper in 1809 and overlaid the sanctum with [[Gold|gold]] leaf in 1830, giving it its name. More than 150,000 people visit each day, and its langar kitchen serves a free vegetarian meal to all visitors. In 1984, [[Indira Gandhi]] sent the Indian Army into the complex during [[Operation Blue Star]], leading to the deaths of thousands of soldiers, militants and civilians. The complex was rebuilt, and it is a nominated [[World Heritage|World Heritage Site]].

Bird of prey (*Aquila chrysaetos*) living in the [[Northern Hemisphere|Northern Hemisphere]], the most widely distributed eagle species. It is dark brown, with lighter golden-brown plumage on the nape; immature birds typically have white on the tail. It hunts mainly [[Hare|hares]], [[Rabbit|rabbits]], [[Marmot|marmots]] and other ground squirrels, using speed, powerful feet and sharp talons. Pairs are monogamous and may stay together for years, returning to large cliff nests. Females lay up to four eggs, incubated for about six weeks, and typically one or two young fledge at about three months. Once widespread across the Holarctic, it has disappeared from many heavily populated areas but remains widespread in [[Eurasia]], [[North America]] and parts of [[North Africa]]. [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] first described it in 1758 as *Falco chrysaetos*.

Wolf-like canid (*Canis aureus*), also called the common jackal, native to [[Eurasia]]. Its coat varies from pale creamy yellow in summer to dark tawny beige in winter. It is smaller than the Arabian wolf, with shorter legs and a more pointed muzzle. Genetic studies indicate it expanded from India around 20,000 years ago, and its oldest known fossil, from Lebanon, is 7,600 years old. It is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and is expanding from southeastern into central Europe. It can produce fertile hybrids with gray wolves. Sulimov dogs, jackal-dog hybrids, are used by Aeroflot for scent detection at Sheremetyevo Airport near [[Moscow]]. Despite its name, it is not closely related to African jackals and is closer to wolves and [[Coyote|coyotes]].

Irrational number, approximately 1.618, denoted φ, that is the positive solution of x² − x − 1 = 0. Two quantities are in the golden ratio if their ratio equals the ratio of their sum to the larger quantity. [[Euclid]] called it the extreme and mean ratio, and Luca Pacioli named it the divine proportion in 1509. It is the ratio of a regular pentagon's diagonal to its side, so it appears in the construction of the [[Dodecahedron|dodecahedron]] and icosahedron. It is also the limit of ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers. Some 20th-century artists and architects, including [[Le Corbusier]] and [[Salvador Dalí]], proportioned works to approximate it, believing it aesthetically pleasing. Attempts to apply it to financial markets are sometimes based on dubious fits to data.

1964 spy film, the third in the James Bond series, directed by Guy Hamilton. Based on the 1959 novel by [[Ian Fleming]], it stars Sean Connery as [[MI6|MI6]] agent James Bond, who investigates gold magnate Auric Goldfinger, whose plan is to irradiate the [[United States|United States]] Bullion Depository at Fort Knox with a dirty bomb. Principal photography took place in the United Kingdom, Switzerland and the United States. The film grossed over $120 million worldwide and was the first Bond film to win an Academy Award, for Best Sound Editing. Its title song was performed by [[Shirley Bassey]]. A Corgi toy of Bond's Aston Martin DB5 became the biggest-selling toy of 1964.

Freshwater fish (*Carassius auratus*) of the [[Carp|carp]] family, native to China, and one of the most popular [[Aquarium|aquarium]] fish. Some carp that are normally gray or silver produce red, orange or yellow mutations. During the [[Tang dynasty|Tang dynasty]] (AD 618–907) people began breeding the gold variety in ponds, and by the [[Song dynasty|Song dynasty]] (AD 960–1279) domestic breeding was firmly established. Fancy-tailed varieties appeared in the [[Ming dynasty|Ming dynasty]]. Goldfish reached [[Japan|Japan]] in 1603, Portugal in 1611 and [[North America|North America]] around 1850. Released goldfish have become invasive pests in parts of North America and Australia. Modern genetic sequencing indicates that domesticated goldfish are varieties of a species native to southern China.

American actress and singer known for lighthearted comedic roles in film and television. She rose to fame on the [[NBC|NBC]] sketch comedy program *Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In* (1968–1970). She received the Academy Award and Golden Globe for Best Supporting Actress for *Cactus Flower* (1969), and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Private Benjamin* (1980). Her other comedies include *Shampoo* (1975), *Overboard* (1987) and *The First Wives Club* (1996). In 2003 she founded the Hawn Foundation, which educates underprivileged children. She has been in a relationship with actor Kurt Russell since 1983.

American multinational investment bank and financial services company, headquartered in [[Manhattan|Manhattan]], New York City. Marcus Goldman founded the firm in 1869 in a one-room basement office. It joined the [[New York Stock Exchange|New York Stock Exchange]] in 1896 and underwrote the 1906 initial public offering of [[Sears|Sears]]. It is one of the largest investment banks by revenue and is ranked 32nd on the Fortune 500 and 19th on the [[Forbes|Forbes]] Global 2000. In 2025, market making supplied 31% of revenue, net interest income 23%, investment and wealth management 20% and investment banking 16%. It is considered a systemically important financial institution. In 2016 it agreed to a $5 billion settlement over misleading investors about residential mortgage-backed securities.

Animated, anthropomorphic being in Jewish folklore, made from clay or mud. The Talmud describes Adam as a golem before he receives life. The best-known legend concerns [[Judah Loew ben Bezalel]], rabbi of [[Prague]] in the late 16th century, who supposedly animated a golem to protect the Jewish community; scholars regard the tale as folklore without contemporary documentation. Kabbalistic texts from the 12th century onward describe ways to animate golems. In modern use, the term denotes any magically created human figure, and golems often appear in [[Video game|video games]]. Because [[Mary Shelley]]'s *Frankenstein* was written in the 1810s, the golem is sometimes treated as a precursor of the Frankenstein monster.

Club-and-ball [[Sport|sport]] in which players hit a ball into holes on a course in as few strokes as possible. A course typically has 9 or 18 holes, each with a teeing ground and a putting green containing the cup, separated by fairways, rough and hazards. Stroke play, counting the lowest total of strokes, is the most common format at all levels; match play compares holes won. The modern game originated in 15th-century [[Scotland|Scotland]], where a 1457 ban by James II is the earliest written record. The 18-hole round was established at St Andrews in 1764. The Open Championship, first played in 1860, is the oldest major tournament. Golf has been an Olympic event since 2016. Its ancient origins are debated, with theories ranging from the Roman game paganica to the Chinese chuiwan.

Membrane-bound organelle found in most [[Eukaryote|eukaryotic]] cells that packages [[Protein|proteins]] into vesicles for transport. It sits where the secretory, lysosomal and endocytic pathways intersect, and contains [[Enzyme|enzymes]] that attach sugar molecules to proteins as they pass through. It is built from flattened membrane sacs called cisternae, typically four to eight per stack, and a mammalian cell contains 40 to 100 stacks. The cis Golgi network receives material from the [[Endoplasmic reticulum|endoplasmic reticulum]], while the trans Golgi network packages proteins for [[Lysosome|lysosomes]], secretory vesicles or the cell surface. Italian biologist Camillo Golgi identified it in 1898 while studying the nervous system; some doubted the discovery until modern microscopes confirmed it. It was named after him in the 1910s.

Legendary [[Philistines|Philistine]] warrior of giant stature in the Bible. In 1 Samuel 17, Goliath challenges the [[Israelites|Israelites]] to send a champion for single combat. The shepherd [[David]] accepts, strikes Goliath's forehead with a stone from a sling, and beheads him with the giant's own sword. An older account in 2 Samuel 21 credits Elhanan, son of Jaare-oregim, with the killing, and scholars consider it the earlier source. The Masoretic text gives Goliath's height as six [[Cubit|cubits]] and a span (about 2.9 m), while the [[Septuagint|Septuagint]] and Dead Sea Scrolls give four cubits and a span (about 2.1 m). The phrase David and Goliath now denotes an underdog contest.
